Stochastic Deep Supervision for Gallery-Consistent Early-Exit Face Recognition

Guray Ozgur Affiliation: TU Darmstadt, Darmstadt, Germany Affiliation: Fraunhofer Institute for Computer Graphics Research IGD, Darmstadt, Germany Email: guray.ozgur@igd.fraunhofer.de    Tahar Chettaoui Affiliation: TU Darmstadt, Darmstadt, Germany Affiliation: Fraunhofer Institute for Computer Graphics Research IGD, Darmstadt, Germany    Eduarda Caldeira Affiliation: TU Darmstadt, Darmstadt, Germany Affiliation: Fraunhofer Institute for Computer Graphics Research IGD, Darmstadt, Germany    Naser Damer Affiliation: TU Darmstadt, Darmstadt, Germany Affiliation: Fraunhofer Institute for Computer Graphics Research IGD, Darmstadt, Germany    Fadi Boutros Affiliation: Fraunhofer Institute for Computer Graphics Research IGD, Darmstadt, Germany
Abstract

Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform strongly in face recognition (FR), yet their fixed-depth inference limits deployment in resource-constrained settings. We propose SD-ViT, a training framework that gives a usable exit at every block depth by making every depth produce discriminative embeddings, for budget-selected fixed-depth exits. Standard ViTs supervise intermediate layers only through backpropagation, so their intermediate representations are not directly optimized to form usable identity embeddings. SD-ViT adds a stochastic auxiliary signal: at each iteration a randomly selected intermediate block is passed through the same embedding head as the final layer and trained with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss. The objective is thus stochastically sampled deep supervision through a shared classifier. Because both loss terms share that head and classifier, intermediate tokens are trained to map into the same embedding space as final-layer tokens. This matters for FR, where matching is by similarity: a probe processed at an early exit can be compared directly against full-depth gallery embeddings, with no gallery recomputation or adaptation layers. On established benchmarks, SD-ViT stays within 0.40.4 IJB-C points of the same backbone trained conventionally at full depth, while its early-exit probes recover over 96%96\% of their own full-depth performance at 50%50\% of the computational cost without modifying the reference gallery. A single verification threshold calibrated at full depth remains usable from quarter depth onward. Code: https://github.com/gurayozgur/SD-ViT.

1 Introduction

FR accuracy is driven by deep networks [22] trained with margin-based softmax objectives [14, 47, 27], and increasingly by ViTs [17], which surpass convolutional backbones on FR benchmarks [13, 30, 31]. A ViT processes every input through a fixed stack of LL blocks at the same cost regardless of input difficulty or device budget, which is at odds with deployment: one model must run from edge processors to datacenter accelerators under budgets differing by orders of magnitude [15]. Compact architectures [10, 5, 51], compression [7] and distillation [23, 33, 28] each yield another static model from a separate run, so covering several budgets means training, storing and switching whole networks. Early-exit networks are the flexible alternative: one model with intermediate classifiers, so inference stops shallow for easy inputs or tight budgets [46, 24]. They were built for closed-set classification, where each exit has its own classifier over a fixed label set and the exits need not share a representation [46, 24, 29]. FR does not fit that template: it is open-set, matching a probe to a gallery of enrolled embeddings by cosine similarity, so independent per-exit heads produce incompatible spaces and a shallow embedding cannot match a full-depth gallery. The closed-set and distillation analogues, per-exit heads that would require re-embedding the gallery at every depth [3] and learned adaptation layers between depths [41], are unattractive here. Galleries can be massive, distributed or privacy-constrained, and adaptation layers break the single-embedding-space assumption enrollment pipelines rely on. Early-exit FR therefore requires that every depth emit embeddings in one shared space, compatible with a gallery enrolled once at full depth.

We address this with Stochastic Deep-supervision for ViTs (SD-ViT), a shared-classifier form of deep supervision (Fig. 1). At each iteration, besides the full-depth output, SD-ViT reads out one auxiliary embedding at a uniformly sampled intermediate block, decodes it with the same head, and scores it against the same prototypes under the same margin-penalty loss. The shared head maps tokens from every depth into one embedding space, and the shared prototypes give each identity a single center in it. Deep supervision is long established [32, 45]. What distinguishes SD-ViT is not that intermediate depths are supervised but through what: the final exit’s own head and classifier instead of exit-specific ones, which makes the embeddings interchangeable across depth. Our controls show that the sampled exit must be trained by the margin loss itself, not by feature matching (Sec. 4.3). At inference a probe may exit at any depth and match a full-depth gallery by plain cosine similarity. Sampling a different block each step spreads supervision uniformly over depth, so every block depth becomes a usable exit after one training run. Sampling is a single-sample estimator of supervising all exits, and Sec. 4.3 finds it on par with deterministic all-exit supervision at one seventh of the auxiliary cost. We contribute: (i) the identification of gallery consistency, one shared embedding space across depths, as the central obstacle to early-exit FR, (ii) SD-ViT, in which a uniformly sampled auxiliary exit shares the final layer’s head and prototypes, making every depth gallery-compatible with no teacher and no adaptation layers, and (iii) evidence that one training run yields a usable exit at every block depth, with full-depth accuracy within 0.40.4 IJB-C points of conventional training, no gallery recomputation, and a single verification threshold usable from quarter depth onward.

2 Related Work

Identity objectives for FR. Margin-penalty softmax losses [14, 47, 30, 6] and auxiliary objectives [48, 21] separate identities and compact each around its center, but only for the final-layer embedding. SD-ViT applies such supervision at a sampled intermediate depth as well, against the prototypes that define the final space.

Deep supervision and knowledge distillation. Deeply-supervised nets [32] and GoogLeNet [45] add auxiliary losses at intermediate layers to aid optimisation and discard the auxiliary heads after training. Knowledge distillation [23] transfers from teacher to student via soft-label or feature-matching objectives, and born-again networks [20] and deep mutual learning [53] remove the fixed teacher. For FR it has used triplet [19], rank-based [28], angular [44] and reverse-feature [33] objectives, and AdaDistill [9] injects teacher-derived class centers into the student margin loss. BYOT [52] combines the two: it attaches auxiliary classifiers to intermediate CNN sections and distills from the deepest into the shallower ones. SD-ViT differs from both lines. Its auxiliary exit is not discarded after training but deployed as an early exit, and it is decoded by the final exit’s own head and scored against the same prototypes instead of a separate classifier. It uses no teacher and no adaptation layers, and couples the exits solely through this shared head and prototypes.

Early-exit and budget-selected inference. Early-exit networks add intermediate classifiers so that easy inputs terminate early [46, 24, 29, 56]. LayerSkip [18] is the closest precedent for our parameter sharing: it trains a language model with layer dropout [25] and an early-exit loss through a shared output head, so intermediate layers become decodable without per-layer heads. Among early-exit ViTs, LGViT [50] uses heterogeneous local-global heads and EnViT [16] exit-aware dropout, both trained by self-distillation. All target closed-set classification, where the label set ties the exits together and nothing forces their representations to be comparable. Open-set FR adds that requirement. Token pruning and merging [39, 4] reduce the cost of each block, not the number of blocks, so they are orthogonal to SD-ViT and could be combined with it. Closest to our setting, ViT-FREE [12] performs training-free early exiting in pretrained ViT-FR models, exploiting constant token dimensionality with a synthetic-data adaptation step, and EX-FIQA [38] fuses intermediate representations for quality assessment. SD-ViT shares the observation that a ViT keeps one dimensionality at every depth, but instead of reading exits from a fixed backbone post-hoc it optimizes every block to produce gallery-consistent embeddings. We compare against both of its settings (Sec. 4.2). Training-free ViT-FREE is precisely our Baseline read-out. ViT-FREEFT trains an exit-specific projection and prototype set per depth. We report it under self-evaluation, the setting it was designed for, and under our gallery-fixed setting.

ViTs for FR. TransFace [13] addresses ViT overfitting with patch-level augmentation and hard-sample mining, Part-fViT [43] adds landmark-driven part tokens, and KP-RPE [31] replaces learnable positional encodings with keypoint-relative ones. All treat the ViT as a fixed-depth backbone for a single full-depth pass, addressing neither multi-exit inference nor gallery-consistent retrieval. SD-ViT adds a stochastic shared-classifier deep-supervision objective that makes every block produce gallery-compatible embeddings, with no change to the inference architecture.

3 Methodology

SD-ViT trains a single ViT-FR model whose every depth produces a discriminative identity embedding. We review the backbone and margin-penalty loss (Sec. 3.1), present SD-ViT (Sec. 3.2), and describe gallery-consistent early-exit inference (Sec. 3.3), Fig. 1 gives an overview.

3.1 Preliminaries

ViT-FR backbone. A ViT-FR backbone [17, 13] splits xx into NN patches, projects each to a dd token, adds positional embeddings, and applies LL pre-normalized blocks z(l)=ℬl​(z(l−1))z^{(l)}=\mathcal{B}_{l}(z^{(l-1)}). A token sequence uu becomes an embedding through the head ℋ\mathcal{H},

e=ℋ⁡(u)=ϕ⁡(vec⁡(LN⁡(u)))∈ℝD,e=\mathcal{H}(u)=\phi\!\left(\mathrm{vec}\!\left(\mathrm{LN}(u)\right)\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, (1)

where LN\mathrm{LN} is a network-wide layer normalization, vec\mathrm{vec} flattens the tokens, and ϕ\phi is an N​d→d→DNd\!\to\!d\!\to\!D projection with batch normalization. We write e^=e/‖e‖\hat{e}=e/\|e\|. The standard setup produces only eL=ℋ⁡(z(L))e_{L}=\mathcal{H}(z^{(L)}).

Margin-penalty softmax loss. The backbone is trained as a closed-set classifier over CC identities [14, 47, 6]. With class prototypes W=[w1,…,wC]W=[w_{1},\dots,w_{C}], ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized columns w^j\hat{w}_{j} and cos⁡θj=w^j⊤​e^\cos\theta_{j}=\hat{w}_{j}^{\top}\hat{e}, the margin-softmax loss is

ℒcls​(e,y)=−log⁡exp⁡(s​ψ​(θy))exp(sψ(θy))+∑j≠yexp(scosθj),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}(e,y)=-\log\frac{\exp\!\big(s\,\psi(\theta_{y})\big)}{\exp\!\big(s\,\psi(\theta_{y})\big)+\sum\limits_{j\neq y}\exp\!\big(s\,\cos\theta_{j}\big)}, (2)

with yy the ground-truth identity, ss a scale and ψ\psi a margin on the target logit (e.g. ArcFace [14] or CosFace [47]). SD-ViT applies to any such ℒcls\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}. We use AdaFace [30] and show in Sec. 4.3 that ArcFace gives the same pattern.

Why intermediate depths are not embeddings. Only eLe_{L} is supervised, intermediate z(l)z^{(l)} receive gradients through backpropagation alone and are never required to be separable or aligned to WW, so reading them out does not yield an embedding matchable against full-depth references.

3.2 Stochastic Shared-Classifier Deep Supervision

Two exits sharing one embedding space. At every training iteration we keep the full-depth (primary) embedding and additionally read out a secondary embedding at a randomly chosen block,

ep=ℋ⁡(z(L)),es=ℋ⁡(z(k)),k∼𝒰⁡{1,…,L−1},e^{\mathrm{p}}=\mathcal{H}\!\left(z^{(L)}\right),\qquad e^{\mathrm{s}}=\mathcal{H}\!\left(z^{(k)}\right),\quad k\sim\mathcal{U}\{1,\dots,L-1\}, (3)

with 𝒰\mathcal{U} uniform over the first L−1L-1 blocks. Both exits are decoded by the shared head ℋ\mathcal{H}, including its LN\mathrm{LN}, and scored against the shared prototypes WW. Exposed to tokens from many depths, one LN\mathrm{LN} and one ϕ\phi must serve every block. Because a ViT keeps token dimensionality N×dN\times d at every block, unlike the changing width of CNN stages, the same head applies unchanged at any depth, with no dimensionality reduction and no per-exit adaptation layers. SD-ViT targets backbones of constant token width, and Sec. 4.3 verifies the objective on a second such backbone, KP-RPE [31].

Weighted dual objective. Both exits are supervised by the same margin-penalty loss, combined with a fixed weight ω\omega:

ℒ=ω​ℒcls​(ep,y)+(1−ω)​ℒcls​(es,y).\mathcal{L}=\omega\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}\!\left(e^{\mathrm{p}},y\right)+(1-\omega)\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}\!\left(e^{\mathrm{s}},y\right). (4)

The primary exit gets the larger weight, keeping full-depth accuracy the principal objective, while the secondary term supervises the sampled depth against the same WW.

Why the exits become comparable. Eq. 4 never asks ese^{\mathrm{s}} to match epe^{\mathrm{p}}: there is no teacher, no detached target and no divergence term between the exits. Both terms are identity-label losses that update the backbone, ℋ\mathcal{H} and WW, and ω\omega only balances them. Whatever aligns the two exits must therefore come from what the two terms share, and we see two candidate effects.

The first is the shared head: ℋ\mathcal{H} is one map, one LN\mathrm{LN}, one projection ϕ\phi and one set of batch-normalization statistics, that must turn the final tokens and the tokens of every sampled block into embeddings the margin loss can separate. At test time ϕ\phi is affine, so eL−eke_{L}-e_{k} is the linear part of ϕ\phi applied to the difference of the two normalized token states. In a pre-norm ViT those states are two snapshots of one residual stream, z(L)=z(k)+∑l>kΔlz^{(L)}=z^{(k)}+\sum_{l>k}\Delta_{l}. Making both discriminative through the same ϕ\phi favors later blocks that refine the identity information ϕ\phi already reads at depth kk, and does not re-encode it, which would keep eke_{k} close to eLe_{L}. Per-exit heads remove this pressure, since each can read identity from a different subspace.

The second is the shared prototypes. ℒcls\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}} depends on ee only through the cosines {w^j⊤​e^}j=1C\{\hat{w}_{j}^{\top}\hat{e}\}_{j=1}^{C} and is minimized by driving e^\hat{e} toward w^y\hat{w}_{y}, so with one WW the embeddings of identity yy at every supervised depth are pulled toward one center. With the head shared, a separate prototype set for the intermediate exits costs about a point (Sec. 4.3). Both come from a single forward pass, since z(k)z^{(k)} is produced en route to z(L)z^{(L)}, so the auxiliary path adds one head-and-classifier evaluation.

Shared statistics and prototype sampling. Three details follow from sharing ℋ\mathcal{H} and WW. (i) The batch-normalization layers of ϕ\phi are traversed twice per step. Each branch is normalized by its own batch statistics and both updates enter the same running estimates, so the deployed statistics mix the final and the sampled depths and one set serves every exit at test time. (ii) With PartialFC [2] both terms of Eq. 4 see the same positive prototypes, since the sampled subset always contains the batch labels. Negatives are redrawn per term, and both terms update the same WW. (iii) AdaFace’s running feature-norm statistics, which set its adaptive margin, are updated by both terms.

3.3 Early-Exit Inference

At test time the model terminates at any depth kk and reads out an embedding through the same head,

ek=ℋ⁡(z(k)),k∈{1,…,L},e_{k}=\mathcal{H}\!\left(z^{(k)}\right),\qquad k\in\{1,\dots,L\}, (5)

where k=Lk{=}L recovers the standard full-depth model.

Gallery consistency. SD-ViT’s defining property for FR is that early-exit probes require no change to the gallery. Since ℋ\mathcal{H} and WW are shared, e^k\hat{e}_{k} lies in the same space as a full-depth gallery embedding, so cosine similarity stays meaningful between a shallow probe and deep references: no per-exit projection, no re-enrollment. The property holds within one model, with probe and gallery from the same network for the constant-width ViTs. An operational system also needs its threshold to survive the change of depth. A ROC-based metric does not establish this, since TAR at a target FAR may pick a different threshold per exit. Sec. 4.4 tests the stronger property: one threshold, calibrated on full-depth development scores, applied unchanged at every exit.

Computational scaling. Exiting at block kk runs kk of LL blocks, cutting backbone computation to about k/Lk/L, while the head runs on all NN tokens at a fixed cost. Choosing kk trades accuracy for latency within one model, with no retraining. Throughout, kk is selected by a compute budget, not per input: we evaluate budget-selected fixed-depth exits, not an input-adaptive policy. A per-image policy is left to future work.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Training data. We train on WebFace4M [57] (4.24.2M images, 206206K ids) and, for scaling, ViT-B on WebFace12M [57] (12.712.7M, 618618K).

Architectures. ViT-S/12, ViT-S/15 and ViT-B/24 on 112×112112\times 112 images, at 18.3718.37/22.9322.93/26.7426.74 full-depth GFLOPs. GFLOPs follow [40], with 8×88\times 8 patches and d=512d{=}512 throughout. The patch embedding and head add the same 0.140.14 GFLOPs at every exit on both backbones, and only the per-block cost differs (1.521.52 ViT-S, 1.111.11 ViT-B).

Loss and training. We adopt AdaFace [30] (m=0.4m{=}0.4, h=0.333h{=}0.333) with the augmentations of [30]: 40 epochs, batch 10241024, AdamW [35] (lr 10−410^{-4}, weight decay 0.050.05), a cosine schedule [34, 49] with 3-epoch warmup, and PartialFC [2, 1] at sampling rate 0.60.6. Unless stated otherwise ω=0.7\omega{=}0.7 (Sec. 3.2). It was chosen on the reporting benchmarks (Tab. 2). An ArcFace [14] variant tests a second margin loss. The auxiliary exit adds 33-6%6\% training time (→68.665.5\!\to\!68.6 A100 GPU-h for ViT-S/12).

Baseline and reference models. Baseline is the same backbone, data, augmentation, optimizer, schedule, PartialFC setting, margin loss, batch and seed as SD-ViT. The only difference is Eq. 4 with ω=1\omega{=}1 and no auxiliary term. Its architecture and per-exit cost are identical, so the differences below isolate the objective. Reading the Baseline’s intermediate blocks through the shared head is exactly the training-free protocol of ViT-FREE [12], so its rows are simultaneously that comparison. Tab. 1 adds ViT-FREEFT and truncated ViTs at matched GFLOPs. ViT-FREEFT follows [12], fine-tuning one projection head per exit with its own classifier on the frozen backbone. For a like-for-like comparison, that backbone is our Baseline and the heads are trained with its data and loss (WebFace4M, AdaFace). It is evaluated under self-evaluation in Tab. 1 and 3, and gallery-fixed in Tab. 5.

Benchmarks and protocol. We report the five high-quality sets [26, 37, 42, 54, 55] by their average, TinyFace [11] Rank-1 and IJB-C [36] TAR@FAR=10−4=10^{-4}. To evaluate exit kk we run the first kk blocks, apply the shared head, ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalize and match by cosine similarity, either between exit-kk embeddings (default) or from an exit-kk probe to a full-depth reference (gallery-fixed). In the latter the enrolled side is always full depth and the querying side exit kk. For IJB-C every image of an enrollment template, the first template of each pair, is embedded at full depth and the rest are probes.

4.2 Early-Exit Recognition across Depths

Tab. 1 and Fig. 2 compare final-exit-only training against SD-ViT. Because a standard ViT never decodes intermediate blocks into embeddings, its early exits collapse: the ViT-S/12 baseline reaches 42.2%42.2\% IJB-C and 56.0%56.0\% TinyFace at half depth, and 11.1%11.1\% and 40.6%40.6\% at quarter depth. SD-ViT reaches 95.1%95.1\%/71.2%71.2\% and 87.0%87.0\%/64.6%64.6\% at those same budgets (9.269.26 and 4.704.70 against 18.3718.37 GFLOPs). The pattern repeats on ViT-B/24 and at scale: on WebFace12M the baseline gives 12.1%12.1\% IJB-C at quarter depth where SD-ViT gives 95.0%95.0\%. Full depth costs a little. IJB-C is 0.380.38, 0.330.33 and 0.130.13 points below the Baseline in the three configurations, and TinyFace on WebFace12M drops 1.181.18 points. There is no inference overhead, since the two architectures are identical.

Against dedicated single-budget models. Tab. 1 also reports ViTs of 33 and 66 blocks trained from scratch at the GFLOPs of SD-ViT’s quarter- and half-depth exits. They are better at their own budget: 93.7893.78 vs. 87.0187.01 IJB-C at 4.704.70 GFLOPs and 95.9495.94 vs. 95.1195.11 at 9.269.26. The trade is not accuracy at one budget but coverage: NN budgets otherwise need NN networks. In FR each has its own embedding space, so a gallery enrolled with one cannot be queried by another. SD-ViT covers every budget in one network against one gallery, giving up 0.830.83 points at half depth to do so.

4.3 Ablation Studies

Ablations use ViT-S/12 on WebFace4M with AdaFace unless stated (Fig. 3, Tab. 2).

Effect of the primary-loss weight ω\omega. Full depth varies at most 0.530.53 points on IJB-C over ω∈{0.5,0.7,0.9}\omega\in\{0.5,0.7,0.9\}, while early exits degrade sharply as ω→1\omega\!\to\!1: half-depth IJB-C falls →→→42.22%95.52\!\to\!95.11\!\to\!93.35\!\to\!42.22\%. At ω=0\omega{=}0 early exits stay strong but full depth drops to 95.25%95.25\% against 96.51%96.51\%, so a dominant primary term is needed. We use ω=0.7\omega{=}0.7.

Margin loss. The gains are not specific to AdaFace. The half-depth IJB-C ArcFace baseline (57.82%57.82\%) is higher than AdaFace’s (42.22%42.22\%), yet SD-ViT brings both to comparable levels, 94.97%94.97\% and 95.11%95.11\%, gains of +37.2+37.2 and +52.9+52.9 points, with full depth within 0.40.4 points of the baseline in both.

Network depth. On a ViT-S/15 the pattern holds: at half depth the baseline reaches 70.81%70.81\% IJB-C and 62.53%62.53\% TinyFace against SD-ViT’s 95.59%95.59\% and 72.0%72.0\%, with full depth preserved (96.7096.70 vs. 96.83%96.83\%).

A second ViT backbone. To check that the objective is not specific to a plain ViT, we repeat it on KP-RPE [31], which replaces learnable positional encodings with keypoint-relative ones and is itself a stronger full-depth model (97.0397.03 vs. 96.8996.89 IJB-C for our baseline). It is an isotropic ViT, so the shared head applies unchanged, and its keypoint-relative encoding adds 0.0180.018 GFLOPs per exit, under 0.4%0.4\% at the depths compared here. Its baseline collapses at early exits as the plain one does (64.7264.72 and 82.9682.96 high-quality average at quarter and half depth, 12.6712.67 and 53.5253.52 IJB-C), while KP-RPE with SD reaches 94.1194.11 and 96.5696.56 there against 93.6893.68 and 96.4296.42 for SD-ViT on the plain backbone, and 88.1988.19 and 95.2795.27 IJB-C against 87.0187.01 and 95.1195.11. At full depth it loses 0.090.09 on the high-quality average and 0.360.36 on IJB-C.

Where and how many exits to supervise. Would fixing the auxiliary exit at one or two depths suffice? Fixing yields a sharply peaked profile (Fig. 3(d)): supervising only block 66 gives 17.9%17.9\% and 38.1%38.1\% IJB-C at exits 22 and 33 against 74.4%74.4\% and 87.0%87.0\% for sampling, which instead spreads supervision over all depths. The fixed variants are better at their chosen depths: {6}\{6\} reaches 96.07%96.07\% at exit 66 against 95.11%95.11\% for sampling, and {3,6}\{3,6\} reaches 91.89%91.89\% against 87.01%87.01\% at exit 33. Under the gallery-fixed protocol {3,6}\{3,6\} also beats sampling at its two depths (94.3394.33 and 95.9795.97 against 93.0693.06 and 95.8495.84). The trade is therefore up to five points at the supervised depths. Away from those depths the fixed variants fall behind (48.7%48.7\% at exit 22 for {3,6}\{3,6\} against 74.4%74.4\%). Committing to {3,6}\{3,6\} is the right choice only if those two budgets are known before training and never change.

Fixed variants are expected to fail where they are not supervised, so they do not by themselves justify sampling. The relevant comparison is deterministic supervision of all L−1L{-}1 intermediate exits, the upper bound sampling estimates. Tab. 3 puts the two within half a point of each other (86.5486.54/95.1595.15 IJB-C against 87.0187.01/95.1195.11, 92.7392.73/95.7995.79 against 93.0693.06/95.8495.84 gallery-fixed). All-exit supervision costs 88.388.3 A100 GPU-h against 68.668.6, i.e. 7.4×7.4\times the auxiliary cost over the 65.565.5 GPU-h baseline (22.822.8 versus 3.13.1). The accuracy therefore comes from shared-classifier deep supervision itself, and sampling is a single-sample, constant-cost estimator of it whose contribution is efficiency.

What has to be shared. Tab. 3 varies the components of Eq. 4 one at a time. Blocks (i) and (ii) are strict controls, each one run from scratch at SD-ViT’s setting except for the marked component. Block (iii) cannot be matched that way, since freezing prototypes at a full-depth solution and fitting per-exit heads on a frozen backbone both presuppose a model trained beforehand. First, the auxiliary exit must be supervised by the margin loss itself: replacing it with a feature-matching MSE onto the model’s own final embedding, keeping the shared head, costs 31.531.5 points at quarter depth (55.4955.49 vs. 87.0187.01). Second, with the head shared, a separate prototype set W′W^{\prime} for the intermediate exits is nearly free (86.9086.90 vs. 87.0187.01 self, 91.7691.76 vs. 93.0693.06 gallery-fixed), so sharing the centers adds about a point. From block (iii), per-exit heads with per-exit prototypes lose the property: ViT-FREEFT falls to 61.7861.78 gallery-fixed at quarter depth against 93.0693.06, and to 16.9316.93 against 59.3159.31 on TinyFace. It changes the head, the prototypes and the training regime together, so it does not isolate the head. The controls thus establish that the sampled exit needs the margin loss itself. Freezing WW at a separately trained full-depth solution improves SD-ViT’s quarter-depth exit (89.9389.93 vs. 87.0187.01 self, 93.4293.42 vs. 93.0693.06 gallery-fixed). Without the sampled exit, the frozen centers alone reach 5.815.81 and 76.7876.78 gallery-fixed at exits 3 and 6, against the baseline’s 0.020.02 and 34.6334.63. Frozen centers thus pull intermediate depths toward the gallery’s space only weakly (18.4818.48 self at quarter depth), and help most combined with the sampled exit.

Comparison with knowledge distillation. Tab. 4 compares SD-ViT with distillation baselines, with and without an external teacher. Each replaces the shared-classifier coupling with a feature-matching term λ​‖e^s−e^t‖22\lambda\|\hat{e}^{\mathrm{s}}-\hat{e}^{\mathrm{t}}\|_{2}^{2} (λ=100\lambda{=}100) added to ℒcls​(ep,y)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}(e^{\mathrm{p}},y) [41, 8], with the teacher ete^{\mathrm{t}} either the model’s own final embedding (Feature-MSE, the variant analysed in Sec. 4.4) or that of the separately trained, frozen Baseline (Feature-MSE (teacher)). KD, teacher MSE applies the same term to the final embedding e^p\hat{e}^{\mathrm{p}} instead. A prototype-level variant initialises WW from that full-depth model and freezes it (frozen full-depth WW), with or without the sampled exit.

Every baseline lifts early exits above the no-auxiliary baseline yet falls short of SD-ViT. At quarter depth SD-ViT reaches 87.0%87.0\% IJB-C against 55.5%55.5\% for the best feature-MSE variant and below 22%22\% for external-teacher distillation. The shared classifier, not feature matching, is what makes early exits work, and an external teacher is unnecessary: prototypes frozen at a separately trained full-depth solution shift quarter-depth IJB-C by under 33 points, while a teacher-to-intermediate MSE is worse than the model’s own target (40.3%40.3\% vs. 55.5%55.5\%). All methods converge at full depth, and SD-ViT trains more cheaply than the teacher-MSE variants, which need a second forward pass (68.668.6 vs. 84.784.7/85.785.7 GPU-h).

4.4 Gallery Consistency

An early-exit probe should match a gallery enrolled once at full depth. The gallery-fixed protocol embeds one element of each pair at the final block and the other at exit kk, so accuracy measures cross-depth matching. We evaluate the baseline, Feature-MSE, ViT-FREEFT and SD-ViT.

Embeddings align across depth. Fig. 2(h) gives the mean cosine similarity between each intermediate embedding and the final one. The baseline’s early embeddings are nearly orthogonal to it at exit 33 (0.140.14) and still far from it at exit 66 (0.400.40). SD-ViT raises this to 0.760.76 and 0.910.91, more than the explicit MSE objective (0.410.41 and 0.640.64).

Recognition against a full-depth gallery. Fig. 2(e-g) and Tab. 5 report recognition against a fixed full-depth gallery. On the high-quality sets the baseline manages 66.8%66.8\% at quarter depth against SD-ViT’s 96.2%96.2\%, and 91.0%91.0\% even at the first exit. The gap widens on harder benchmarks: the baseline is unusable below half depth (0.0%0.0\% TinyFace and 0.0%0.0\% IJB-C at quarter depth) where SD-ViT reaches 59.3%59.3\% and 93.1%93.1\%.

One threshold across all depths. TAR at a target FAR is a ROC-level statistic: it permits a different threshold at every exit, so Tab. 5 alone does not show that a deployed system can keep its threshold when it starts exiting early. We split each benchmark’s pairs once into a development and a test half, choose a single τ\tau on the development half of the full-depth scores at the target FAR, and apply it unchanged at every exit on the test half. Tab. 6 reports the realized FAR and TAR against a τ\tau re-calibrated per exit. On IJB-C at FAR=10−4=10^{-4}, τ=0.382\tau{=}0.382 costs SD-ViT 0.190.19 points of TAR at exit 99, 0.640.64 at exit 66 and 3.973.97 at quarter depth, so half depth needs no recalibration. The baseline cannot be operated this way. It gets nothing at exits 11 and 33, 19.59%19.59\% against 34.19%34.19\% with a per-exit τ\tau at exit 66, and becomes operable only by exit 99 (90.6190.61 against 92.1692.16). Its usable range under a fixed threshold thus begins three quarters of the way down the network. Realized FAR shrinks as the probe gets shallower and stays below the target at every early exit. At exit 11, however, even SD-ViT keeps only 15.66%15.66\% against 63.81%63.81\% with a per-exit τ\tau. The single-threshold property therefore holds from quarter depth onward, not at every exit. We ran this calibration on ViT-S/12 only.

5 Conclusion

We presented SD-ViT, a stochastic shared-classifier deep-supervision framework that turns a standard ViT into a face recognizer with a usable exit at every block depth. A uniformly sampled intermediate block is decoded by the same head and scored against the same prototypes as the final layer, with no teacher and no per-exit adaptation layers. An early-exit probe therefore matches a gallery enrolled once at full depth by plain cosine similarity, with a single verification threshold held fixed from quarter depth onward. Across ViT-S and ViT-B on WebFace4M and WebFace12M, SD-ViT stays within 0.40.4 IJB-C points of the identically trained baseline at full depth while recovering over 96%96\% of its own full-depth accuracy at half the computation. Our controls show that the sampled exit needs the margin loss itself, not feature matching. Future work includes input-adaptive per-image exit policies.

Supplementary Material

The main paper mostly presents the quarter-, half-, and full-depth operating points and the average of the five high-quality verification sets, whereas here we give per-exit results on the individual benchmarks, together with the cost and parameter accounting, the training budget of the runs, and the per-dataset gallery-consistency analysis.

Notation. Throughout, “Exit kk” denotes terminating inference after the first kk transformer blocks and decoding the resulting tokens with the shared embedding head (Sec. 3 of the main paper). Unless noted otherwise, all per-exit results use the self-evaluation protocol (probe and gallery embedded at the same exit), the gallery-fixed protocol of Sec. S9 instead matches an exit-kk probe against a final-block gallery. “HQ (5)” is the average of LFW, AgeDB-30, CFP-FP, CPLFW, and CALFW.

Appendix S1 Computational Cost and Training Budget

Computational cost. Table S1 lists the exact per-exit cost and the size of the network retained when the model is pruned at each exit.

Training budget. Table S2 lists the wall-clock training cost of every run in A100 GPU-hours. The stochastic auxiliary loss term processes a single additional intermediate exit per step and adds only a few percent of overhead, it adds no inference-time cost, since the deployed network is architecturally identical to the baseline.

Appendix S2 Full Per-Exit Results on WebFace4M

Tables S3 and S4 give the complete per-exit breakdown for the two backbones of Fig. 2 (top row) and Tab. 1, on all eight evaluation protocols: the five high-quality verification sets individually (and their average), TinyFace Rank-1 and Rank-5, and IJB-C at all three operating points (10−510^{-5}, 10−410^{-4}, 10−310^{-3}). The pattern summarized in the main paper holds on every benchmark: the baseline degrades severely as the exit is moved earlier, while SD-ViT degrades far less (ViT-S/12 IJB-C 40.3240.32 at exit 1 and 87.0187.01 at exit 3, against 96.5196.51 at full depth). The gap is largest at the early exits (up to 76.076.0 IJB-C points, at exit 3 of ViT-S/12) and closes near full depth, where the baseline is slightly ahead (from exit 11 of ViT-S/12 and exit 21 of ViT-B/24).

Appendix S3 Scaling to WebFace12M

Table S5 gives the full per-exit breakdown for ViT-B/24 trained on the larger WebFace12M. Larger-scale training improves both models at full depth, but does not by itself make the baseline’s intermediate layers usable: at quarter depth the WF12M baseline still collapses (e.g. 12.1%12.1\% TAR at 10−410^{-4} on IJB-C), while SD-ViT reaches 95.0%95.0\% there.

Appendix S4 Loss-Function Ablation: ArcFace

We repeat the ViT-S/12 experiment with ArcFace in place of AdaFace. Table S6 gives the full per-exit breakdown for both the ArcFace baseline and ArcFace SD-ViT. The pattern matches the AdaFace case: SD-ViT lifts the early exits far above the baseline (80.6080.60 vs. 61.0461.04 HQ (5) at exit 1, 93.7193.71 vs. 68.0468.04 at exit 3) and stays within 0.30.3 points of it at full depth (97.2097.20 vs. 97.4197.41 HQ (5), 96.6596.65 vs. 96.9396.93 IJB-C), with the first two exits still short of full depth as on AdaFace.

Appendix S5 Primary-Loss Weight

Tables S7-S9 give the full per-exit breakdown for the remaining values of the primary-loss weight ω\omega studied in Fig. 3(a) and Tab. 2, the chosen ω=0.7\omega{=}0.7 run is Table S3 (SD-ViT block) and ω=1.0\omega{=}1.0 is the baseline. Increasing ω\omega trades early-exit accuracy for full-depth accuracy (full-depth IJB-C 96.2096.20, 96.5196.51 and 96.7396.73 at ω=0.5\omega{=}0.5, 0.70.7 and 0.90.9, against 96.8996.89 for the baseline). ω=0.0\omega{=}0.0, which supervises only the sampled early exit, keeps early exits strong but lowers full-depth IJB-C to 95.2595.25.

Appendix S6 Network Depth: ViT-S/15

Table S10 gives the full per-exit breakdown for the deeper ViT-S/15 backbone (the mid- and full-depth summary is in Sec. 4.3 of the main paper).

Appendix S7 Where to Supervise

Section 4.3 of the main paper argues that stochastically sampling the auxiliary exit is preferable to supervising one or two fixed depths. Tables S11 and S12 give the full per-exit breakdown of the two fixed-exit variants (the stochastic counterpart is Table S3, SD-ViT block). Supervising at fixed exits produces a sharply peaked profile that is strong at and after the chosen depth but collapses earlier, most visibly for the exit-{6}\{6\} variant, whose IJB-C TAR at exit 2 is only 17.9%17.9\% versus 74.4%74.4\% for stochastic sampling. The fixed variants are stronger at their chosen depths: the {3,6}\{3,6\} variant reaches 91.89%91.89\% IJB-C at exit 3 against SD-ViT’s 87.01%87.01\%, and under the gallery-fixed protocol, reported in Table 3 of the main paper, it supervises both of its depths better than sampling does (94.3394.33 and 95.9795.97 against 93.0693.06 and 95.8495.84).

Appendix S8 Auxiliary Objectives

Sec. 4.3 and Tab. 4 of the main paper compare SD-ViT against auxiliary objectives along two axes: whether a method uses an external pretrained teacher, and whether it targets early-exit usability. This section gives the per-exit breakdown behind those two columns: external-teacher variants in Table S13, feature-matching variants in Table S14, and the two that bring the teacher to the sampled exit in Table S15. The Baseline and SD-ViT rows are in Table S3. All runs use ViT-S/12 on WebFace4M with AdaFace. Every feature-matching baseline replaces the shared-classifier coupling by

ℒ=ℒcls​(ep,y)+λ​‖e^s−e^t‖22,λ=100,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cls}}(e^{\mathrm{p}},y)+\lambda\big\|\hat{e}^{\mathrm{s}}-\hat{e}^{\mathrm{t}}\big\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\lambda=100, (S1)

with the margin loss applied to epe^{\mathrm{p}} only and e^t\hat{e}^{\mathrm{t}} either the model’s own final embedding (Feature-MSE) or that of the Baseline, trained separately and frozen (Feature-MSE (teacher)). In both, the sampled exit receives no label loss. KD, teacher MSE applies the same term to the final embedding, with e^p\hat{e}^{\mathrm{p}} in place of e^s\hat{e}^{\mathrm{s}}, i.e. standard embedding distillation into a single-exit student. The prototype-level variant instead freezes WW at the separately trained full-depth solution (frozen full-depth WW). Table S14 additionally separates two placements of the MSE that the main paper does not distinguish: pre-proj. matches the token sequences before ϕ\phi, and post-proj. matches the embeddings after it. The post-projection variant is the Feature-MSE of the main paper and the one analyzed in Sec. S9. Matching before the projection is worse in 9696 of the 9999 per-exit entries at exits 1 to 9 (the exceptions are CFP-FP and IJB-C at 10−310^{-3} at exit 7 and TinyFace R-5 at exit 9), by up to 38.538.5 IJB-C points (exit 4), and the two placements are within about a point of each other from exit 10 on.

Appendix S9 Gallery Consistency: Full Results

Tables S16 and S17 give the full per-exit gallery-fixed results behind Sec. 4.4 and Tab. 5: an exit-kk probe matched against a gallery embedded at the final block. A value of 0.000.00 is a genuine collapse, not a missing entry.

Appendix S10 Embedding Alignment Across Depth

Tables S18-S20 give the per-dataset cosine similarity between each intermediate embedding and the final-block embedding, for each of the three models and each of the seven test sets. The main paper plots their average (Fig. 2(h)). SD-ViT has the highest similarity on every dataset and at every exit. The baseline’s early embeddings are nearly orthogonal to its final embedding (at most 0.260.26 up to exit 3), and the explicit-MSE variant lies between the two, except on TinyFace at exits 1, 9 and 10, where it is below the baseline. At exit 11 all three are within 0.040.04.

Appendix S11 Comparison with ViT-FREE and Matched-Compute Models

Sec. 2 and Sec. 4.1 of the main paper explain why training-free ViT-FREE coincides with our Baseline read-out, and Tab. 1 and Tab. 5 give its headline numbers. ViT-FREEFT follows the original method: one projection head per exit, fine-tuned with its own classifier while the backbone stays frozen. For a like-for-like comparison, the backbone is our ViT-S/12 Baseline and the heads are trained with its data and loss (WebFace4M, AdaFace), at exits {1,3,6,9,12}\{1,3,6,9,12\}. Table S21 reports both protocols at those exits. Table S22 lists the matched-compute references discussed in Sec. 4.2: ViT-S backbones of 33 and 66 blocks trained from scratch with the identical setting.

Sec. 4.3 compares stochastic sampling against deterministic supervision of all L−1L{-}1 intermediate exits, loss =0.7ℒ(e(L))+0.3⋅1L−1∑k<Lℒ(e(k))=0.7\,\mathcal{L}(e^{(L)})+0.3\cdot\frac{1}{L-1}\sum_{k<L}\mathcal{L}(e^{(k)}), with the same shared head, prototypes and ω\omega. Table S23 gives that run per exit under both protocols.

Table 3 of the main paper is summarized at two exits. Table S24 gives the separate-intermediate-W′W^{\prime} control per exit under both protocols. Per-exit heads are covered only by ViT-FREEFT (Sec. S11), which changes the head and the prototypes together.

Appendix S14 One Threshold Across Depths

Sec. 4.4 defines the protocol: one τ\tau calibrated on a development half of the full-depth scores and applied unchanged at every exit on the held-out half. Table S25 extends Tab. 6 to exit 1 and lists the realized FAR and the mean genuine and impostor scores, and Fig. S1 shows the score distributions behind it. The calibration was run on ViT-S/12 only.

Appendix S15 Measured Latency and Memory

Table S1 reports estimated GFLOPs and parameter counts. Because a FLOP count need not translate into wall-clock savings, Table S26 adds measured batch-1 latency and peak memory per exit on named hardware, for all three configurations. SD-ViT and the Baseline share an architecture, so these numbers apply to both.

Appendix S16 A Second ViT Backbone: KP-RPE

The objective requires a backbone whose token dimensionality is constant across depth, so that one head can decode every exit (Sec. 3.2 of the main paper). This section reports a second backbone that satisfies it. Sec. 4.3 reports the KP-RPE result, Table S27 gives it per exit. Its GFLOPs are measured for this backbone, not copied from the plain ViT: the keypoint-relative encoding projects the five keypoints into the per-block, per-head attention biases once per image, adding 0.0180.018 GFLOPs at every exit, +1.1%+1.1\% at exit 1 falling to +0.1%+0.1\% at full depth.
